newsitem.title: USA: Treasury says New York dealer violated rules.
newsitem.headline: Treasury says New York dealer violated rules.

text.p: The Treasury Department said Thursday that New York securities dealer Lehman Brothers had admitted unintentionally violating rules for participating in government auctions last year.

But the Treasury said it was not imposing any penalties because it found no evidence that Lehman was attempting to manipulate market prices. The Treasury said it was satisfied with corrective measures Lehman has taken voluntarily.

The Treasury is sensitive to any bending of its rules because huge potential profits stand to be reaped by participants in the multi-billion-dollar sales of government securities. The rules were tightened after a scandal in 1990-91 in which Salomon Brothers committed serious bidding violations.
Salomon paid hundreds of millions of dollars in fines and was temporarily suspended as a primary dealer from bidding in government auctions.
The New York Federal Reserve noted problems with Lehman's reporting of some of its holdings in certain securities and contacted Lehman about it in May 1995.

The Treasury said one error resulted in Lehman receiving an amount of a government security at auction that, added to its net long position before the sale, would have given it 40.2 percent of the security and so exceeded the 35 percent limit set by The Treasury. A net long position represents potential ownership or control of a security.
Owning more than 35 percent of an issue is considered likely to give the holder too much sway over prices.

Lehman said it "committed only clerical errors that did not violate the spirit of Treasury's rules aimed at preventing undue concentration" of ownership. But it said it "sincerely regrets" the errors and had taken steps to avoid a recurrence.
